learn.title: A string is a char array
learn.body: A C string is a row of `char` bytes ending with a 0 byte, written `'\0'`. There is no string type. A `char *` pointing at the first letter is how code usually holds a string. Everything you learned about pointers applies.

learn.title: Walking to the end
learn.body: This prints `5 5`. `p` moves one char at a time until it meets the 0 byte. The count and the pointer difference both give the length. The 0 byte is not counted, so the string uses 6 bytes.

learn.title: Tracing the loop
learn.body: The string is `"hi"`, stored as h, i, 0.
steps: `p` starts at h, which is not 0, so `p++`, length 1
`p` is at i, not 0, so `p++`, length 2
`p` is at the 0 byte, so the loop stops

learn.title: Literals are read-only
learn.body: `char *s = "hello";` points at text stored by the program. Changing it with `s[0] = 'J';` is undefined behavior and often crashes. To get a copy you may change, use an array: `char t[] = "hello";`. Then `t[0] = 'J';` is fine and gives `Jello`.
`strlen` from `string.h` does the walk for you and does not count the 0 byte. For `"hello"` it returns 5, while `sizeof` of the array is 6.

questions.prompt: What byte ends every C string?
questions.explanation: The 0 byte tells code where the string stops.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does the array holding `"hello"` use, including the end byte?
questions.explanation: Five letters plus the 0 byte make 6.
`strlen` counts the letters before the 0 byte.

choices: The address of the first letter
questions.explanation: `s` is a pointer to the first char.
String literals should be treated as read-only.

questions.prompt: Which gives you text you can safely change?
questions.explanation: The array form makes your own writable copy of the bytes.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of finding a string's length in order.
steps: If not, move `p` forward and count 1
Stop at the 0 byte and report the count
questions.explanation: Repeat the check and move steps until the 0 byte appears.
